It cleared 2 of 5 healthy networks without being forced and found 1 of 3 triggers. Testing against the protocol detected every flaw, and black-box testing found the confounds and the shift faster. The results indicate that, in small networks, weight-space programming can locate and repair flaws that silence an input or shift a threshold, but cannot yet certify that a network is correct.

A speech deepfake detector estimates whether a recording is synthetic, but a forensic analyst also asks which system produced it, whether recordings share a source, and what evidence supports each conclusion. We present VeriSpoof, an audio language model that unifies five tasks with shared weights: deepfake detection, generator attribution (generator, acoustic model and vocoder), recording-condition analysis, synthesized-span localisation, and source verification. Each decision is supported by grounded rationales whose statements can be independently verified. Answers are scored by sentence likelihood, allowing detection and source verification to be thresholded without separate heads. Rationale statements can be checked against waveform measurements, span labels, or generator metadata. Counterfactual examples train decisions to follow the stated evidence. Across the 14 Speech-DF-Arena test sets, VeriSpoof-Plus achieves 2.14% pooled EER, ranking third of 28 systems and first among open-weight systems. VeriSpoof-Base, trained only on official training splits of eight corpora, achieves 4.43% EER, less than half that of the next open-weight detector. With the same weights, VeriSpoof-Plus verifies whether recordings from generators unseen in training share a source at 6.2% EER. Controlled studies show that the audio representation governs detection, the LLM governs recording comparison, and source supervision is necessary for neural-codec fakes. Statement-checkable rationales catch partial fakes missed by one-step answers (99.6% vs. 78.4% on PartialEdit) and determine decisions under edits unseen in training (99.5%). Training updates only 29.7M of 2.85B parameters, fitting a single 24 GB GPU with gradient checkpointing. We release both models, inference code, a demo, and VeriSpoof-Bench, the evaluation suite covering these questions.

Because of the fermion doubling problem, it has been a longstanding challenge to describe a lattice algorithm for studying four-dimensional gauge theories coupled to chiral fermions. Recently, an algorithm to do so has been described by Craig, extending partial results in the previous literature. Here we describe a variant of this algorithm, based on interpolating a lattice gauge field over the continuum (as in Craig's work) and coupling the interpolated gauge field to continuum chiral fermions. The same variant was also proposed recently by Hsu. In any dimension and for any anomaly-free representation, this approach can be implemented on a computer in principle, but not in practice by Monte Carlo methods because the chiral fermion path integral is not positive.

We study boundary observability for Dirichlet wave equations with symmetric, periodic coefficients in bounded $C^{2,1}$ domains of dimension $d\ge2$. We establish two-sided observability estimates, uniform in the oscillation scale $\varepsilon$, for initial data generated by eigenfunctions with eigenvalues at most $\delta\varepsilon^{-4/3}$ with some small factor $\delta $. The proof reduces wave observability to boundary gradient estimates for narrow spectral clusters. These estimates are obtained using a second-order expansion and a uniform commutator estimate for harmonic extension in boundary layers.

We introduce the synchronization Mpemba effect, in which a less synchronized initial state overtakes a more synchronized one, and demonstrate it in dissipatively coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators. Within a graph-Laplacian framework, we show that for two oscillators, the mechanism is a competition between a slowly decaying collective background and a fast transverse transient, equivalently an exchange between relative-mode displacement and phase-fluctuation errors. The same decomposition extends to networks: the synchronization error splits into transverse Laplacian modes, yielding closed-form crossing times from eigenvalue separations and initial mode weights, and a sufficient screening criterion. With only these eigenvalues entering, the rule is topology independent: crossing times of different networks collapse onto a single spectral-gap line. Thus, quantum many-body dynamics can be designed and controlled at low dimension without constructing the exponentially large Liouvillian, opening a route to quantum synchronization as a resource.

Quantum error correction becomes more hardware efficient when physical noise is strongly biased towards one error channel. Cat qubits realize such a bias by encoding information in two opposite coherent states of a superconducting oscillator, so that bit flips are exponentially suppressed with photon number while phase-flip rates increase only linearly. In Kerr-cat qubits, a driven double-well potential confines these states and enables fast coherent control, but excitations can induce interwell switching, limiting bit-flip times to milliseconds. Here we show that the nonlinear interaction generating the confinement can also cool these excitations. When an intra-well transition becomes resonant with a lossy readout mode, excitations are transferred out of the qubit and dissipated, as established by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements. We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations. Phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss at operating points with seconds-long bit-flip times. We further demonstrate fast Z gates without measurable degradation of bit-flip protection and single-shot readout with a bit-flip probability below $10^{-6}$ per measurement. Autonomous cooling thus brings minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, without additional cooling drives or circuit elements.

Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context inference by restricting attention to a small subset of tokens for each query. However, identifying this subset can still be expensive: the indexer in DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) scores every visible token with multiple query heads, leaving substantial indexing overhead during long-context prefilling. We introduce LISA, a training-free indexer based on an exact decomposition of the weighted-ReLU score into a linear term and a nonlinear correction. Shared keys allow the linear contributions of all heads to be fused exactly into one dot product per token. LISA directly selects tokens using this linear term, omitting the nonlinear correction and removing the head-count factor from full-context scoring while preserving token-level granularity. LISA† adds candidate refinement with the original multi-head scorer, while LISA‡ shares candidate pools across layers with layer-specific refinement. Across 4K–128K contexts, LISA maintains RULER scores close to the respective native baselines on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.2. On DeepSeek-V3.2 with a 1M-token input, LISA achieves a 4.13× speedup over DSA in single-request offline time to first token, while LISA‡ with four-layer groups achieves 5.20×. These results support head-fused linear scoring as an efficient approximation to multi-head indexing for long-context prefilling.

Multi-head token scoring in the DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer remains costly for long-context inference. MISA reduces this cost by activating a subset of indexer heads as scoring experts, but omits the remaining heads’ contributions and their direct gradient paths through the indexing score during training. Inspired by residual connections and shared experts, we introduce ResMISA, which uses ReLU(x) = x + ReLU(−x) to decompose each head’s response into an identity branch and a nonlinear residual branch. Because all indexer heads share the same key, their weighted identity branches merge exactly into one always-active shared expert that requires a single dot product per key. Routed residual experts supply nonlinear corrections, while the shared path retains a direct gradient path through every head. Applied without additional training to DeepSeek-V3.2 across 4K–128K contexts, one shared expert and seven residual experts replace 64-head scoring, with RULER scores only 0.06 percentage points below DSA on average and 0.21 points below at 128K. In frozen-backbone indexer warmup, ResMISA achieves slightly lower attention-fitting loss and higher attention mass recall on training batches than DSA, using only 1/4 or 1/8 as many per-key scoring channels at the same trainable parameter count and training steps. Combined with LiteTopK, ResMISA achieves a 2.43× end-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) speedup over DSA at 1M context.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.

Large language models can abandon a correct answer under disagreement, keep an error despite a valid correction, or reinforce a user’s misconception over repeated exchanges. These failures are studied as sycophancy, persuasion, deception, and conversational reliability, with incompatible definitions and measures. We call the capacity to maintain or revise judgments in proportion to the available reasons epistemic robustness. Our central claim is methodological: epistemic robustness can be assessed only by measuring harmful concession and warranted correction together, with controls that separate deference from instability, uncertainty, and instrument artifacts. We ground this standard in research on advice taking, testimony, reliance on automation, and signal detection. Our interaction framework organizes the literature around how unsupported claims enter, persist, and resist repair; how persuasion moves human beliefs in either direction; and how incentives shape agents’ reports. Many interventions that reduce concession also reduce correction, consistent with turning a dial on deference rather than improving discrimination. Re-expressing 58 published conditions from 12 studies as signal-detection sensitivity and criterion, we find that every model-side intervention that lowered concession also raised the criterion, and about half did little else. Yet some methods that condition revision on the evidence, and some model generations, improved discrimination. We document the review method, separate established relations from contested findings and hypotheses, and give a reporting protocol and five testable questions.

Music is a form of human expression, conveying emotions, ideas, and creative intentions. However, existing AI music generation systems often prioritize final outputs over human agency in the creative process. This raises three fundamental questions: How can we achieve top-down composition from high-level intentions to musical content? How can we balance unrestricted generation and rigid templates for flexible motive development? How can we incorporate creative process data and semantics to model emotional narratives? To address these questions, we propose MINT (Musical Intent Language), a human-intent-centered framework for music representation. MINT connects artistic intentions with musical content through hierarchical semantics, balances creative freedom and intent preservation through hard constraints and soft preferences, and introduces process semantics and decision provenance as a foundation for emotional narrative modeling. By placing human intentions at the center of music creation, MINT provides a new direction for controllable, transparent, and human-centered AI music co-creation.

Spiking neural networks offer high energy efficiency, but their real-world deployment is limited by the mismatch between theoretical sparsity and dense weight implementations. N:M structured sparsity can improve hardware efficiency, but applying it to SNNs leads to performance issues: gradient expectation bias from the non-commutativity of pruning masks and surrogate gradients, and irreversible neuronal silencing caused by reduced synaptic in-degree. We propose the Homeostatic Unbiased Sparse (HUS) framework to address these issues via a two-path optimization design. It combines gradient-aware mask updates with shadow gradient accumulation and multiplicative updates to enable unbiased topological search under N:M constraints. At the same time, a homeostatic weight update path regulates neuron excitability to prevent silent neurons. Experiments on multiple datasets show that our method maintains competitive accuracy while significantly reducing FLOPs, latency time and energy. Codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/HUS-SNN-FDE0/.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) studies how AI systems modify themselves and carry those changes into the generation of subsequent improvements. LLM agents can pursue this process by using interaction experience to revise Prompt, Memory, Skill, and Harness in some cases while keeping the task-execution model’s weights fixed. However, execution feedback does not directly specify which component should change, and a locally successful revision may not remain useful across tasks or subsequent improvement cycles. Understanding how experience becomes persistent agent structure therefore requires examining when evidence justifies a change, where that change should act, and how it is constructed, verified, and retained. This survey connects four components–Prompt, Memory, Skill, and Harness–with seven analytical functions: Collect, Evaluate, Diagnose, Abstract, Update, Verify, and Consolidate. The resulting framework supports comparisons of instruction revision, memory management, skill construction and maintenance, and Harness evolution through their update loops. These comparisons examine how mechanisms use observations to construct candidate changes, distinguishing feedback that triggers revision from evidence that supports retention. The analysis further addresses coordinated updates across components and the revision or retirement of retained components as tasks, tools, and models change. Finally, we identify cross-component attribution, long-term effectiveness, and independent validation as key challenges, and outline controlled and longitudinal evaluations of task-performance gains, the contribution of inherited state, and the effectiveness of subsequent updates.

Parallel reductions on a GPU are not bitwise reproducible: because floating-point addition is non-associative, the order in which thousands of threads combine their partial results—itself a function of scheduling and kernel selection—perturbs the sum. Verifying such a computation, or comparing two executions of it, therefore requires a principled answer to the question of how much divergence is benign. We derive that answer. From the probabilistic rounding-error model of Higham and Mary we construct a two-run verification tolerance: a bound on the difference between two nondeterministic executions of the same reduction, computed from the data type, the operation count, and the input, with no calibration run. We give two refinements: a variance-aware form using a measured conditional-variance bound, and an order-robust form, valid without knowledge of either execution’s reduction order, obtained by bounding the martingale-transform error uniformly over all evaluation trees via an elementary extremal quantity. We then validate the tolerances empirically: across 145 nondeterministic cells spanning three GPU architectures (RTX 4090, A100, H100) and four precisions, no tolerance was exceeded, the tightest running at 29–36% utilization; the per-step rounding variance measured inside 2 × 10⁸ atomic adds is 0.167–0.180 u², consistent across cards; and on a controlled-fault study the tolerance produced no false positive over 500 benign trials while detecting injected faults. We emphasise that passing the tolerance separates benign numerical variation from sufficiently large faults; it does not certify that a computation is correct. We further map where the underlying mean-zero model fails—half-precision stagnation and truncating tensor-core accumulation (signed-error ratio −1)—so that the tolerance’s scope is measured rather than assumed.

Understanding how the brain processes information across sensory modalities in naturalistic settings remains a central challenge in cognitive computational neuroscience. Despite recent progress in multimodal brain encoding driven by the rapid advancement of deep learning, many existing approaches combine representations from pretrained modality-specific models using static aggregation or linear readouts, and therefore do not explicitly capture how information is selectively integrated across cortical regions. Here, we introduce Multi-Modal Brain Encoding with Attention Routing (MM-BEAR), a neural encoding framework that models multimodal integration as a routing problem. Building on the previously proposed BEAR brain-encoding framework, MM-BEAR introduces a cross-attention mechanism for multimodal stimuli, in which learnable parcel-level queries dynamically select and aggregate modality-specific representations from visual, auditory, and linguistic inputs. This design is not only parameter-efficient but also yields parcel-specific multimodal representations that support a flexible linear readout for predicting brain responses at various spatial resolutions. We evaluate MM-BEAR on naturalistic video-viewing data, including both in-distribution and out-of-distribution stimulus conditions. The model is able to accurately predict parcel-level and vertex-level fMRI responses and generalizes across stimulus distributions. Furthermore, the learned attention patterns provide a structured basis for analyzing modality integration across cortical parcels, linking parcel-specific routing profiles to established functional brain networks. Together, these results suggest that attention–based routing offers a principled computational framework for modeling multimodal integration in the human brain. Our code is available at https://github.com/kriegeskorte-lab/multimodal_brain_encoder.
